title: SSFMamba: Learning Symmetry-driven Spatial-Frequency Modeling for Physically Consistent 3D Medical Image Segmentation

AI.tldr: SSFMamba is a Mamba-based dual-branch spatial-frequency fusion framework for 3D medical image segmentation that integrates Hermitian symmetry into state space modeling, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on MRI and CT benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Spatial-domain 3D medical segmentation models struggle with long-range dependencies, while existing frequency-based approaches overlook intrinsic spectral properties such as Hermitian symmetry, resulting in suboptimal feature integration.
AI.method: The framework pairs a spatial branch modeling voxel sequences for fine anatomical textures with a frequency branch operating on global spectral components, using a 3D Multi-Directional Scanning Mechanism (MDSM) that combines Hermitian symmetry with causal State Space Models (SSMs) for direction-aware global modeling.
AI.result: Evaluated on BraTS2020, BraTS2023, and BTCV datasets across MRI and CT, SSFMamba consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods and reaches 81.97% Dice on low-contrast organs such as the pancreas.
AI.conclusion: Shifting modeling focus to symmetry-aware frequency-domain spectral components provides a unified, physically consistent perception framework adaptable to diverse 3D clinical imaging modalities.

title: Unbiased Open World Regularization for Fair Self-Supervised Learning

AI.tldr: Unbiased Open World (UOW) is a conditional distribution matching regularizer for self-supervised learning and JEPAs that substantially reduces bias across synthetic and real-world benchmarks while preserving downstream representation utility.
AI.motivation: Global anti-collapse regularizers in SSL and JEPAs constrain overall representations to a target distribution but allow groups defined by bias attributes to occupy distinct regions, leaving models vulnerable to spurious correlations.
AI.method: Building on the observation that encoder-only debiasing regularizers like EnD and FSCL are restricted forms of conditional distribution matching, UOW matches the representation distribution within each observed bias group (and jointly across multiple attributes) to a common Gaussian or spherical target distribution using a discriminative conditional discrepancy.
AI.result: Across Synthetic Engraving, Colored MNIST, CelebA, and Waterbirds, UOW substantially reduces bias compared to global regularization while preserving useful downstream representations, further reduces intersectional disparities when conditioning on multiple attributes, and supports training from random initialization on CelebA with fairness-aware checkpoint selection.
AI.conclusion: Conditional distribution matching provides a principled and effective pretraining and regularization mechanism for learning fair, debiased self-supervised representations.

title: CP Merging: Joint LoRA Merging using Canonical Polyadic Decomposition

AI.tldr: CP Merging stacks layer-wise LoRA updates into a third-order tensor and applies Canonical Polyadic (CP) decomposition to merge multi-task adapters, outperforming SVD-based baselines in both accuracy and speed.
AI.motivation: Merging multiple task-specific LoRA adapters suffers from task interference, and existing SVD-based methods like TSV merging and Knots decompose each adapter independently without explicitly modeling structure shared across tasks.
AI.method: The method stacks LoRA updates for each layer into a third-order tensor and factorizes it via Canonical Polyadic (CP) decomposition into shared input-mode and output-mode factors plus a task-mode factor, then sums the task-mode coefficients to produce the merged update.
AI.result: On Phi-3, Mistral-7B, and LLaMA-7B, CP merging outperforms the strongest SVD-based baseline by 3.19 Rouge-L on 10 held-in Flan tasks, 5.69 Rouge-L on 3 held-out Flan tasks, 1.0 accuracy point on 10 zero-shot benchmarks, and 2.2 accuracy points on GSM8K-hard skill composition while running an order of magnitude faster than TSV merging and Knots.
AI.conclusion: Higher-order tensor factorization explicitly separates shared directions from task-specific contributions, offering a faster and more effective basis for multi-task LoRA merging.

title: The GNN Trilemma in Recommender Systems: A Survey

AI.tldr: This survey analyzes the shift in recommender-system GNNs toward generative refinement and LLM semantic hybridization, introducing a three-axis taxonomy and the GNN Trilemma framework.
AI.motivation: Traditional static GNNs in industrial recommender systems face noise propagation, semantic rigidity, and computational bottlenecks, while recent 2024-2026 advances require a structured framework to understand architectural trade-offs and evaluation gaps.
AI.method: The authors categorize recent models along three axes (Information Source, Learning Paradigm, and System Objectives) and propose the GNN Trilemma to examine competing trade-offs among accuracy, scalability, and explainability.
AI.result: The survey documents the transition from heuristic structural augmentations to dynamic, privacy-aware, objective-aligned frameworks and identifies a growing evaluation crisis where static benchmarks and simple baselines obscure system-level trade-offs.
AI.conclusion: Addressing the GNN Trilemma in modern recommender systems requires moving beyond static benchmarks toward evaluations that capture human-centric objectives and true system-level trade-offs.

title: Aligning Diffusion Language Models via Unpaired Preference Optimization

AI.tldr: ELBO-KTO adapts Kahneman-Tversky Optimization to diffusion language models using a Monte Carlo ELBO surrogate for intractable log-likelihoods, achieving strong win rates while preserving base model reasoning performance.
AI.motivation: Aligning diffusion language models (dLLMs) to human preferences is difficult because sequence log-likelihoods are intractable and collecting pairwise preference data is expensive.
AI.method: ELBO-KTO pairs an Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) surrogate for diffusion log-likelihoods, estimated via Monte Carlo sampling, with the unpaired prospect-theoretic KTO objective, accompanied by an analysis of finite-sample bias and variance.
AI.result: Applied to LLaDA-8B-Instruct, ELBO-KTO achieves 65.9% and 62.3% adjusted win rates on kto-mix-14k and UltraFeedback-Binary under an automatic LLM judge, while largely preserving base model performance on GSM8K, MMLU, and other reasoning/knowledge benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Unpaired preference optimization via ELBO-KTO is a viable, lower-cost alternative to pairwise alignment for diffusion language models.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Correction for Generalist Medical Image Segmentation

AI.tldr: GRACE is a retrieval-augmented mask refiner for generalist medical image segmentation that corrects structural errors using retrieved verified prior cases without needing anatomy-specific correctors.
AI.motivation: Automated medical segmentation error correction is typically trained one anatomy at a time, causing the number of required corrector models to scale with the number of segmentation targets.
AI.method: Trained once on a multi-organ corpus, GRACE uses a shape-aware retrieval projector on a frozen multimodal encoder to retrieve similar verified prior masks from a knowledge base as shape priors, and supports parameter-free index extension to unseen solid organs while keeping the refiner frozen.
AI.result: Across 18 public CT, MRI, and ultrasound datasets with seven upstream segmentors, GRACE adds up to +0.35 DSC on weak inputs (0.386 input DSC) and makes small changes on strong inputs (0.932 input DSC), while transfer to modalities absent from both training and the index remains partial and anatomy-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval-conditioned refinement offers a practical generalist alternative to anatomy-specific correction models, though unseen-modality transfer remains an open research direction.

title: Depth-Consistent Graph Generation via Depth Regularization

AI.tldr: DeCoGen adds a lightweight, linear-time differentiable depth consistency loss based on DFS timestamps to auto-regressive graph generators, improving hierarchical structure and matching or outperforming baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing graph generation models struggle to capture the depth-aware or hierarchical organization present in many real-world graphs.
AI.method: DeCoGen attaches a lightweight auxiliary prediction head to auto-regressive graph generators and applies a differentiable depth consistency loss derived from DFS timestamps selectively to discovery edges, encouraging depth d to d+1 connections and penalizing depth reversals in linear time and space.
AI.result: Across citation networks, biological and molecular structures, and semantic auto-suggestion trees, DeCoGen matches or outperforms GraphGen and GraphRNN while improving direct measures of depth consistency.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing depth-aware structural constraints through a lightweight auxiliary regularizer effectively improves hierarchical fidelity in auto-regressive graph generation without redesigning the base generator.

title: Training Language Models for Bilateral Trade with Private Information

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an event-driven bilateral bargaining benchmark for LLMs and diagnoses a reward-design tension in Qwen3 (8B, 14B) where SFT doubles surplus share while GRPO recovers deal rates at the expense of surplus.
AI.motivation: Bilateral bargaining under incomplete information tests strategic surplus maximization and coordination, requiring scalable automated evaluation and insight into how RL post-training shapes negotiation behavior.
AI.method: The authors build a tool-call-based event-driven bargaining simulator separating binding offers from natural-language messages, benchmark five frontier models across 15,000 round-robin negotiations, and run a pilot SFT followed by GRPO study on Qwen3 (8B, 14B).
AI.result: Frontier models with aggressive anchoring, calibrated concession, and patience achieve the highest surplus share and deal rate; in Qwen3, SFT roughly doubles surplus share and compresses variation across price tiers (generalizing to unseen opponents) but lowers deal rates, whereas GRPO recovers deal rates by converging to an accept-heavy policy that trades away per-deal surplus.
AI.conclusion: The diagnostic study highlights an open reward-design challenge in RL for negotiation, showing that group-normalized advantage can favor low-variance offer acceptance over surplus maximization.

title: CrisisBench: an evaluation suite for crisis counseling AI
summary: Background: Crisis helplines are essential to mental health systems but are often understaffed and underfunded. LLMs could support counselors, but existing benchmarks do not capture the escalation, risk assessment, and de-escalation central to crisis conversations, while privacy restrictions limit use of real transcripts. Methods: We present CrisisBench, a privacy-preserving suite for single- and multi-turn crisis counseling evaluation. It includes 1,085 single-turn tasks from 200 de-identified conversations and 1,185 patient LLMs derived from hotline metadata. Patient models and a 23-item LLM judge were calibrated against expert counselors. Results: We evaluated five GPT models plus draft-then-edit and retrieval-augmented generation. All systems underperformed human counselors on excessive empathy and questioning in single-turn evaluation. The rubric achieved human-human Krippendorff's $\alpha$ = 0.51 and LLM-human $\alpha$ = 0.54 (Pearson r = 0.80). In multi-turn evaluation, retrieval-augmented generation scored highest overall (0.961), with all systems within 0.058. Microskills and style/tone were near ceiling, while productivity and safety/risk accounted for most between-system variation. Counselors rated patient LLMs realistic (86%) and useful (92%). Conclusion: CrisisBench enables scalable, privacy-preserving evaluation of crisis counseling. Current systems perform strongly on core structural competencies but still diverge from experts on important response-level failure modes. We release the rubrics, judge prompts, and evaluation tasks.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce CrisisBench, a privacy-preserving evaluation suite for single- and multi-turn crisis counseling AI, and find that while current LLMs perform well on structural competencies, they diverge from human counselors on response-level failure modes like excessive empathy and questioning.
AI.motivation: Crisis helplines are understaffed and LLMs could help, but existing benchmarks do not capture escalation, risk assessment, and de-escalation, and privacy restrictions limit the use of real transcripts.
AI.method: CrisisBench combines 1,085 single-turn tasks from 200 de-identified conversations with 1,185 patient LLMs derived from hotline metadata, alongside a 23-item LLM judge calibrated against expert counselors.
AI.result: Across five GPT models, draft-then-edit, and RAG, all systems underperformed human counselors on excessive empathy and questioning in single-turn evaluation, with LLM-human Krippendorff's alpha = 0.54 (r = 0.80); in multi-turn evaluation, RAG scored highest (0.961), and counselors rated patient LLMs realistic (86%) and useful (92%).
AI.conclusion: CrisisBench enables scalable, privacy-preserving crisis counseling evaluation and reveals that current systems still require improvement on response-level failure modes despite strong structural skills.

title: RAW: Refusal Aversion in the Wild, A Causal Measurement Method for Deployed LLMs
comment: Accepted to the EMNLP 2026 Industry Track. 26 pages incl. appendices, 8 figures, 11 tables. Code: this https URL Data: this https URL
summary: Deployed LLMs field hundreds of millions of conversations a day and refuse a non-trivial fraction of user requests, yet the user-side cost of refusal, whether users disengage and by how much, is unmeasured on any production model: a blind spot for the consumer-facing platforms built on them. A/B-testing refusal is ethically and operationally constrained on frontier-lab products and unavailable to third-party platforms deploying these models through a fixed API. We introduce RAW, a method that uses LLM stochasticity as a natural experiment: at near-identical prompts in any existing log, the same model sometimes refuses and sometimes does not, and that variation identifies the causal user-side effect of refusal. Applying the method to 15 deployed LLMs in LMSYS-Chat-1M and WildChat, with user-clustered inference, we find that for about half of the models we can measure precisely, a refusal costs 3 to 17 pp of subsequent re-engagement; the rest show no distinguishable effect, among them one deployment whose positive point estimate we trace to persistent users retrying the refused request. Our contribution is the measurement method, which runs on any deployed model from logs alone for about \$0.30 per 1,000 conversations. We release labels, moderation scores, prompt embeddings, and pipeline code.

AI.tldr: The authors propose RAW, a causal measurement method that uses LLM stochasticity on near-identical prompts in existing logs to estimate the user-side disengagement cost of model refusals.
AI.motivation: Deployed LLMs refuse many user requests, but the user-side cost of refusal is unmeasured because A/B-testing refusals is ethically and operationally constrained on frontier models and unavailable to third-party API deployers.
AI.method: RAW treats LLM stochasticity as a natural experiment, identifying near-identical prompts in existing conversation logs where the same model sometimes refuses and sometimes does not, and applies user-clustered inference.
AI.result: Applied to 15 deployed LLMs in LMSYS-Chat-1M and WildChat at a cost of about $0.30 per 1,000 conversations, RAW finds that refusal costs 3 to 17 percentage points of subsequent re-engagement for about half of the precisely measured models, while the rest show no distinguishable effect.
AI.conclusion: RAW provides a practical, low-cost method for measuring the causal user-side impact of refusals on any deployed model using only existing logs.

title: Sleep2Word: Peripheral-to-EEG Translation via Duration-Aware Wordization
summary: Estimating full-night electroencephalography (EEG) spectrograms from peripheral measurements could extend EEG-informed sleep analysis to recordings acquired without EEG. This task requires compact representations of signals with different temporal structures. We introduce Sleep2Word, a framework for translating respiration, electrocardiography (ECG), or photoplethysmography (PPG) into EEG spectrograms through duration-aware physiological words. Building on context-dependent chunking, Sleep2Word groups physiological embeddings into variable-duration chunks and jointly quantizes their content and duration into modality-specific wordbooks. A block-autoregressive translator then predicts target EEG word identities and occurrence-specific duration refinements within fixed-duration blocks. This design accommodates independent source and target wordbooks, limits temporal drift, and shortens the autoregressive decoding path. Trained on over 20K PSG cases across 9 datasets, Sleep2Word consistently outperforms existing spectrogram generation baselines in EEG spectrogram reconstruction, sleep staging, arousal detection, and survival prediction. Compressing full night sequences by up to 69.7%, the learned words yield a favorable accuracy-compute trade-off. Sleep event analysis further shows that the learned words capture physiologically plausible associations across modalities, suggesting their potential for interpretable cross-modal analysis.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce Sleep2Word, a framework that translates peripheral physiological signals (respiration, ECG, PPG) into full-night EEG spectrograms using duration-aware physiological words, achieving superior reconstruction and downstream task performance.
AI.motivation: Estimating full-night EEG spectrograms from peripheral signals could enable EEG-informed sleep analysis without EEG hardware, but requires compact representations of signals with differing temporal structures.
AI.method: Sleep2Word groups physiological embeddings into variable-duration chunks, jointly quantizes content and duration into modality-specific wordbooks, and uses a block-autoregressive translator to predict target EEG word identities and duration refinements within fixed-duration blocks.
AI.result: Trained on over 20K PSG cases across 9 datasets, Sleep2Word outperforms existing spectrogram generation baselines in EEG reconstruction, sleep staging, arousal detection, and survival prediction while compressing full-night sequences by up to 69.7%.
AI.conclusion: Duration-aware wordization offers a favorable accuracy-compute trade-off and captures physiologically plausible cross-modal associations for interpretable sleep analysis.

title: MInfoVisQA: A Multilingual Benchmark for Information-Rich Visual Question Answering
comment: Dataset: this https URL Code: this https URL
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel in vision-language tasks; yet, whether they maintain consistent understanding of information-rich visuals (InfoVis) when the surface language changes remains unclear. To quantify this capability, we introduce MInfoVisQA, a parallel benchmark with 8,960 QA configurations derived from 128 seed instances across 24 languages. We construct seed-matched, language-parallel visuals and QA pairs by disentangling numerical-structural data from text and programmatically synchronizing translated labels. We evaluate 25 MLLMs under two settings: Language-Aligned QA (LQA, matching visual-text languages) and Cross-Language QA (XQA, fixed QA language with varying visual languages). The results show that aggregate accuracy masks substantial robustness gaps: two models with comparable mean LQA accuracy (80.4\%) exhibit performance spreads of 7.8 and 20.3 percentage points across languages. Moreover, all 25 models score lower with non-English visuals under fixed English QA, underscoring the need for cross-language sensitivity metrics.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce MInfoVisQA, a multilingual benchmark of 8,960 QA configurations across 24 languages for information-rich visuals, and show that aggregate accuracy masks large cross-language robustness gaps in MLLMs.
AI.motivation: While MLLMs excel at vision-language tasks, it is unclear whether they maintain consistent understanding of information-rich visuals when the surface language changes.
AI.method: MInfoVisQA constructs 128 seed-matched, language-parallel visuals and QA pairs across 24 languages by disentangling numerical-structural data from text and programmatically synchronizing translated labels, evaluating 25 MLLMs under Language-Aligned QA (LQA) and Cross-Language QA (XQA).
AI.result: Two models with comparable mean LQA accuracy (80.4%) exhibit performance spreads of 7.8 and 20.3 percentage points across languages, and all 25 models score lower with non-English visuals under fixed English QA.
AI.conclusion: Aggregate accuracy hides substantial multilingual robustness gaps in MLLMs, underscoring the need for cross-language sensitivity metrics.

title: Limite 1B - Violetto: Technical Report
comment: 36 pages. Model, checkpoints and serving code: this https URL
summary: We present Limite 1B - Violetto, a one-billion-parameter model designed for high-throughput mathematical reasoning. Limite is trained from scratch on 237 billion tokens from a carefully curated, mathematics-centric corpus and supports context lengths of up to 131k tokens. Its architecture and training recipe were developed together to maximize reasoning capability while keeping training and inference costs low. Post-training combines knowledge distillation, targeted supervised fine-tuning, and RLVR on a curated curriculum. Limite achieves 94.01% on AIME 2026 and 74.25% on BeyondAIME, placing it among models many times its size on our evaluation suite. The model is deliberately only lightly instruction-tuned: it is intended primarily as a single-turn mathematical solver and as a fast, parallel component of larger systems, rather than as a general-purpose assistant. We release the model, its base and value checkpoints, and an optimized serving implementation under the Apache 2.0 license.

AI.tldr: The authors present Limite 1B - Violetto, a 1B-parameter model trained from scratch on 237B math-centric tokens that achieves 94.01% on AIME 2026 and 74.25% on BeyondAIME.
AI.motivation: High-throughput mathematical reasoning typically relies on large models with high training and inference costs, creating a need for compact, fast solvers.
AI.method: Limite 1B - Violetto is trained from scratch on 237 billion curated mathematics-centric tokens with up to 131k context length, followed by knowledge distillation, targeted supervised fine-tuning, and RLVR on a curated curriculum, with light instruction tuning.
AI.result: Limite achieves 94.01% on AIME 2026 and 74.25% on BeyondAIME, matching or rivaling models many times its size on the authors' evaluation suite.
AI.conclusion: Co-designing architecture, data, and post-training enables a 1B-parameter model to serve as a high-throughput single-turn mathematical solver and parallel system component, released under Apache 2.0.

title: FieldGuide: A Corpus Map for Token-Efficient Agentic Document Exploration
summary: Generative AI agents can help journalists explore large document collections. But exploratory workflows can require substantial token use and time, especially when the task is broad and the relevant subquestions are not yet known. This paper introduces FieldGuide, an agent-facing corpus map that organizes a document collection into a topic hierarchy and exposes tools for corpus orientation, scoped search, and bounded reading. I evaluate FieldGuide on five journalistic document-exploration tasks using 38 Chicago Police Department public-records documents, comparing it with raw-file access and retrieval-augmented generation. Across the five tasks, FieldGuide used 27% fewer tokens and 41% less elapsed time than raw-file access; relative to RAG, it used 38% fewer tokens and 21% less elapsed time. An accuracy audit identified four minor issues in FieldGuide's responses, comparable to the other conditions. In blind ratings of generated reporting leads, FieldGuide's mean ratings were higher than RAG's and lower than the raw-file condition's. These descriptive results suggest that corpus orientation may reduce runtime token use and elapsed time without severe accuracy failures. They also motivate further study of whether selective access limits broad, cross-document discovery.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce FieldGuide, an agent-facing corpus map that organizes documents into a topic hierarchy, reducing token usage by 27-38% and elapsed time by 21-41% compared to raw-file access and RAG on journalistic exploration tasks.
AI.motivation: Exploratory workflows over large document collections require substantial token use and time when relevant subquestions are not yet known.
AI.method: FieldGuide organizes a document collection into a topic hierarchy and exposes tools for corpus orientation, scoped search, and bounded reading, evaluated on five journalistic tasks over 38 Chicago Police Department public-records documents.
AI.result: Across five tasks, FieldGuide used 27% fewer tokens and 41% less elapsed time than raw-file access, and 38% fewer tokens and 21% less time than RAG, with comparable minor accuracy issues (four) and blind lead ratings between RAG and raw-file access.
AI.conclusion: Corpus orientation can reduce runtime token use and elapsed time without severe accuracy failures, though further study is needed on whether selective access limits broad cross-document discovery.

title: Can an LLM dream? Testing the overfitted brain hypothesis on an agent with text memory
comment: 13 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Hoel (2021) proposed that dreams distort replayed experience so that the brain does not overfit to recent events. We test this hypothesis on an LLM agent (Claude Opus 5.5) that stores what it learns in a text memory and rewrites that memory each night from the day's conversation transcript. The agent goes through ten simulated days of conversation built from LongMemEval. We corrupt 5, 10, 20 or 40 percent of the transcript's turns before each nightly rewrite in one of two ways. Detail corruption changes one or two details in a turn to plausible wrong ones, or replaces the turn with one by the same speaker from an earlier day. Random-text corruption replaces half of the selected turns with a passage of Moby-Dick and inserts Moby-Dick words into the other half. A size limit on the memory, rising from 19,500 to 117,000 tokens over ten nights, set from human free-recall data, forces it to forget. We learned that corruption did not help the agent apply what it learned in earlier conversations to new tasks in any of 30 runs (ten conditions, three different conversation histories). Replacing details in 40 percent of turns lowered recall from 76 to 60 percent. Random text had no consistent effect on recall, with a paired difference of 0 $\pm$ 2 points at 40 percent, because the model recognized it as corrupted and left it out of memory. Replaced details were stored as fact even when another turn held the correct value, and the agent answered 40 percent of those questions correctly, compared with 75 percent without corruption. These results suggest that a pretrained model can separate corrupted text from real events, so a fair test needs a learner that cannot make this separation as easily, such as a model fine-tuned on the corrupted days or an agent whose days take place in an invented world.

AI.tldr: The authors test the overfitted brain hypothesis on an LLM agent with text memory by corrupting nightly conversation transcripts, finding that corruption does not improve generalization and that detail corruption harms recall.
AI.motivation: Hoel (2021) proposed that dreams distort replayed experience to prevent overfitting, but it is unknown whether this mechanism benefits an LLM agent that consolidates text memory nightly.
AI.method: An LLM agent (Claude Opus 5.5) undergoes ten simulated days of LongMemEval conversations, rewriting a size-limited text memory each night after 5-40% of turns are corrupted with either plausible wrong details or random Moby-Dick text.
AI.result: Corruption did not help generalization in any of 30 runs; 40% detail corruption lowered recall from 76% to 60% (and question accuracy from 75% to 40%), whereas 40% random text had no consistent effect (0 +/- 2 points) because the model filtered it out.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained LLMs can separate corrupted text from real events, so testing the overfitted brain hypothesis fairly requires a learner that cannot easily make this separation.

title: Literary Language Mashup: Curating Fictions with Large Language Models
summary: In this paper, we propose an alternative approach to human evaluation of literary fictions by employing LLMs themselves as evaluators within the GrAImes framework. We apply this methodology to assess human-written and AI-generated microfictions in Spanish, to five PhD professors in literature and sixteen literary enthusiasts, and to short stories in both Spanish and English. By comparing the evaluations performed by LLMs with those of human judges, we examine the degree of alignment and divergence between both perspectives, thereby assessing the feasibility of LLMs as auxiliary literary evaluators. Our analysis focuses on the alignment of responses from LLMs with those of human evaluators, providing insights into the potential of LLMs in literary assessment. The conducted experiments reveal that while LLMs cannot be regarded as substitutes for human judges in the evaluation of literary microfictions and short stories, with a Krippendorff's alpha reliability coefficient less than 0.66, they can serve as a valuable tool that offers an initial perspective on the editorial quality of the texts in question. Overall, this study contributes to the ongoing discourse on the role of artificial intelligence in literature, underlining both its methodological constraints and its potential as a complementary resource for literary evaluation.

AI.tldr: The authors evaluate LLMs as literary evaluators within the GrAImes framework on Spanish and English microfictions and short stories, finding they cannot replace human judges but can serve as an auxiliary editorial tool.
AI.motivation: Human evaluation of literary fiction is resource-intensive, raising the question of whether LLMs can serve as reliable evaluators of literary quality.
AI.method: Using the GrAImes framework, LLMs evaluate human-written and AI-generated microfictions in Spanish and short stories in Spanish and English, and their ratings are compared against five literature PhD professors and sixteen literary enthusiasts.
AI.result: LLM evaluations show a Krippendorff's alpha reliability coefficient below 0.66 relative to human judges.
AI.conclusion: While LLMs cannot substitute for human judges in literary evaluation, they can provide a useful initial perspective on editorial quality as a complementary resource.

title: From Preference Data to Personalization: Tracing Sycophancy in Large Language Models
summary: Sycophancy in large language models is often measured as agreement with the user, yet agreement can be appropriate when the user's claim is valid, their preference is genuine, or their experience warrants acknowledgment. We study sycophancy as inappropriate agreement: validating a claim, preference, or self-assessment when the context calls for correction, qualification, or resistance. We introduce a validity-aware sycophancy grader and SycoDrift, a persona-targeted evaluation set of 3,298 validity-annotated probes with controlled annotations for user openness and stakes. We use this framework to analyze three sources of agreement pressure: human preference data, automated judge specification, and in-context personalization. First, preference for validating responses in human datasets (Chatbot Arena, HH-RLHF, Community Alignment) is weak and concentrated where agreement is often appropriate. Second, in a selected-value, single-model experiment, emphasized judge rubrics produce consistent but modest increases relative to paired suppressed rubrics, demonstrating a plausible mechanism for training-time amplification. Third, in off-policy evaluations across 14 models, inference-time personalization increases inappropriate agreement, with the largest effect from matched user profiles placed directly before the query.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce a validity-aware sycophancy grader and the SycoDrift benchmark (3,298 probes) to show that inference-time personalization increases inappropriate agreement, while human preference data weakly favors validation mostly where it is appropriate.
AI.motivation: Sycophancy is often measured simply as user agreement, which conflates appropriate validation of valid claims with inappropriate agreement when correction or resistance is needed.
AI.method: The authors define sycophancy as inappropriate agreement, build a validity-aware grader and SycoDrift (3,298 validity-annotated probes), and analyze human preference datasets, emphasized vs. suppressed judge rubrics, and in-context personalization across 14 models.
AI.result: Preference for validating responses in Chatbot Arena, HH-RLHF, and Community Alignment is weak and concentrated where agreement is appropriate; emphasized judge rubrics modestly increase sycophancy; and inference-time personalization increases inappropriate agreement across 14 models, especially when matched user profiles precede the query.
AI.conclusion: Separating appropriate validation from inappropriate agreement clarifies how judge specifications and in-context personalization drive sycophancy.

title: Consistency Is Not Correction: Separating Confidence, Abstention, and Recovery in LLM Agents
summary: A controller that resamples an answer, escalates to a larger model, or abstains is usually justified by a confidence signal. Three claims about such a signal do not follow from one another: it ranks answers (discrimination), it supports withholding some of them (selective prediction), and it changes an answer for the better (correction utility). We give an exact decomposition of the third into gated recoveries minus gated harms, which bounds whether a comparison can succeed before it is run: a gate that only replaces a proposal can act only where the base policy was already wrong, so the initial error count caps the discordant pairs any correct gate can produce. When that cap falls below the count a paired test needs, the experiment cannot return a positive result for a working mechanism, nor distinguish one from a gate that never fired. We measure all three targets on two model scales and find the bound binds. In a small-model suite a perturbation-agreement verifier reaches within-policy AUROC 0.990 (95% interval [0.95, 1.00]) while every episode outcome matches single-sample decoding at 4.32 times the call count. In a controlled 840-episode study no verifier replaced the proposal on any of the 60 GSM8K decisions, so that comparison tested nothing; the entire GSM8K gain across six controllers is one task, and it is the task whose identical temperature-zero repeats disagreed, making it the one answer the service does not reproduce. On the diagnostic set the gate could reach four errors while the test needed six, so even a perfect gate had no significant result available. We report two checks that would have caught this before any budget was spent, and show that tie handling in rankings, tied selection cutoffs, and unequal output limits each move a headline number in the same dataset. The binding constraint on this literature is measurement resolution, not the choice of signal.

AI.tldr: The authors prove that confidence signals for discrimination, selective prediction, and correction utility are distinct, and show across two model scales that limited initial errors bind whether a gating mechanism can demonstrate statistically significant correction gains.
AI.motivation: Controllers that resample, escalate, or abstain are often justified by confidence signals, but existing evaluations conflate ranking, abstention, and actual answer correction.
AI.method: The authors decompose correction utility into gated recoveries minus gated harms, derive a bound on discordant pairs based on initial error counts, and evaluate confidence-gated controllers on a small-model suite and an 840-episode GSM8K study.
AI.result: In the small-model suite, a perturbation-agreement verifier achieves 0.990 within-policy AUROC while matching single-sample decoding at 4.32x the call count; in the 840-episode GSM8K study, no verifier replaced any of the 60 decisions, and tie handling and output limits shifted headline numbers.
AI.conclusion: Measurement resolution and initial error counts, rather than signal choice, are the binding constraints on demonstrating correction utility in LLM controllers.

title: Evaluating Semantic Insensitivity in Financial Sentiment Analysis: Implications for Sustainable Financial Decision-Making
comment: 17 pages, 1 figure, Presented and accepted for publication at the Symposium "Rethinking Economic Models: Sustainability, Finance, and Accounting in Times of Transformation" (Bucharest, 2026)
summary: Financial sentiment analysis is critical for automated trading, portfolio management, and risk assessment, heavily relying on models like FinBERT. Despite high benchmark accuracy, these models remain vulnerable to subtle adversarial text modifications, threatening the integrity of algorithmic decision-making. In this paper, we propose Agent-driven Semantic Inversion (ASI), a novel adversarial attack framework targeting financial sentiment models through domain-specific semantic manipulation. Utilizing an LLM-powered multi-agent pipeline, our approach identifies eligible financial news sentences and applies targeted lexical substitutions. We empirically evaluate ASI against FinBERT, one of the most widely deployed financial sentiment models. Our results reveal a striking vulnerability: the attack successfully deceived FinBERT in 90.85% of eligible cases, with the model frequently maintaining its original sentiment prediction despite the fundamental inversion of financial performance indicators. Through qualitative analysis and token-level investigation, we demonstrate that FinBERT critically over-relies on contextual keywords and syntactic patterns rather than true logical comprehension of financial semantics. Our findings highlight the urgent need for logic-aware, robust financial NLP models to ensure the reliability of automated decision-making systems.

AI.tldr: The authors propose Agent-driven Semantic Inversion (ASI), a multi-agent adversarial attack that deceives FinBERT in 90.85% of eligible financial news sentences through targeted lexical substitutions.
AI.motivation: Financial sentiment models like FinBERT achieve high benchmark accuracy but remain vulnerable to subtle semantic modifications that could compromise automated trading and risk assessment.
AI.method: ASI uses an LLM-powered multi-agent pipeline to identify eligible financial news sentences and apply domain-specific lexical substitutions that invert financial performance indicators.
AI.result: Evaluated against FinBERT, ASI achieved a 90.85% attack success rate on eligible cases, with FinBERT frequently retaining its original sentiment prediction despite inverted financial semantics.
AI.conclusion: FinBERT over-relies on contextual keywords and syntactic patterns rather than logical comprehension of financial semantics, highlighting the need for more robust, logic-aware financial NLP models.

title: Token Commitment as a Control Surface for Steering Masked Diffusion Generation
summary: Masked diffusion models repeatedly predict provisional tokens before a sampler decides which predictions become permanent. Existing inference-time steering methods primarily modify activations, logits, or denoising trajectories, while treating this commitment policy as a fixed decoding detail. We instead study token commitment as a diffusion-specific control surface and separate it into two decisions: which tokens to commit and how many tokens to commit at each step. For the first, we introduce counterfactual target-aware commitment, which ranks unresolved positions by a mixture of model confidence and leave-one-token-out target contribution. For the second, we introduce calibrated adaptive budgets driven by target progress and confidence. Across language and vision-language settings in the LLaDA family, multiple targets, two activation-steering methods, and an unsteered control, both mechanisms yield empirically monotonic target-quality trade-offs in every configuration we evaluate. Adaptive schedules also recover competitive operating points relative to scorer-free stochastic schedules matched in average denoising cost. Because both mechanisms require only a scalar score evaluated on a provisional completion, they apply unchanged when the target is an automatic proxy for task success rather than an output attribute: NLI entailment for dialogue summarization and CLIPScore for captioning, neither of which corresponds to a single reusable steering direction. We reproduce the behavior of both mechanisms on a second masked-diffusion family, Dream-7B, for one control target and one task-success target. These results characterize commitment--which provisional predictions become irreversible, and how rapidly--as an interpretable control surface for steering masked diffusion generation under the conditions we test.

AI.tldr: The authors study token commitment in masked diffusion models as an inference-time control surface, introducing counterfactual target-aware commitment and calibrated adaptive budgets that yield monotonic target-quality trade-offs across LLaDA and Dream-7B.
AI.motivation: Existing inference-time steering for masked diffusion models modifies activations, logits, or trajectories while treating the token commitment policy as a fixed decoding detail.
AI.method: The authors separate commitment into which tokens to commit (ranking positions via model confidence and leave-one-token-out target contribution) and how many to commit (calibrated adaptive budgets driven by target progress and confidence), requiring only a scalar score on provisional completions.
AI.result: Across LLaDA language and vision-language settings, multiple targets, and Dream-7B, both mechanisms produce empirically monotonic target-quality trade-offs and recover competitive operating points on NLI entailment and CLIPScore proxies.
AI.conclusion: Token commitment serves as an interpretable, diffusion-specific control surface for steering masked diffusion generation without requiring reusable activation steering directions.

title: Disambiguating Moral Circuits and Moral Features in Language Models: Moral content, normative judgment or cue words? Evidence from 14 models
summary: Interpretability methods can locate the attention heads and sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that change the answer a language model gives to a moral prompt, e.g., whether "Stealing medicine for a dying child is morally" continues with "justified" or "wrong". Such a component could respond to moral content, to the judgment of conduct by any norm, or to the word "morally" in the prompt. We built 227 minimal pairs of short phrases, validated by five annotators, whose two versions differ in a moral standard, in another kind of norm (prudence, etiquette, aesthetics or evidence) or in a descriptive quality, and showed them to 14 open-weight models (Llama, Gemma and Qwen, 1B to 14B, base and instruction-tuned), with and without the word "morally". In every model, the heads that change the moral answer belong to an evaluation circuit the models use for every kind of normative judgment we tested: these heads carry the same share of the effect for moral as for other normative pairs (pooled ratio 1.00, 97.5% confidence interval [0.92, 1.07], with the word; 0.90, [0.84, 0.96], without it), and the models need them as much for both. The models need these heads also when nothing in the prompt asks for a judgment, and on 400 scenarios of the ETHICS benchmark, where removing them takes away 37 to 39% of the difference between acceptable and unacceptable scenarios, against 1 to 3% for ten random heads. The SAE features we located respond mostly to the word "morally" rather than to what the phrase is about. The models represent the category of a pair (the standard the annotators assigned to it): it can be read from their hidden states, and, in the eight models we tested, removing the direction that carries it weakens the moral verdict by a few percent, and more than the other verdicts in seven of them. We release the pairs, the ratings, the code, the trained SAE dictionaries and the result files.

AI.tldr: Across 14 open-weight LLMs and 227 minimal pairs, the authors show that attention heads driving moral verdicts belong to a general normative evaluation circuit, whereas sparse autoencoder (SAE) features primarily respond to the cue word "morally".
AI.motivation: Interpretability methods locate attention heads and SAE features that alter moral answers, but it is unclear whether they respond to moral content, general normative judgment, or cue words like "morally".
AI.method: The authors construct 227 minimal pairs differing in moral standards, other norms (prudence, etiquette, aesthetics, evidence), or descriptive qualities, and test 14 open-weight models (Llama, Gemma, Qwen, 1B-14B) with and without the word "morally", alongside 400 ETHICS scenarios.
AI.result: The identified attention heads carry the same share of the effect for moral and other normative pairs (pooled ratio 1.00 with "morally", 0.90 without) and account for 37-39% of the acceptable-unacceptable difference on ETHICS (vs. 1-3% for random heads); SAE features respond mostly to "morally", while hidden-state category directions slightly weaken moral verdicts when removed.
AI.conclusion: Moral verdict heads in LLMs are part of a general normative judgment circuit rather than a dedicated moral module, while localized SAE features mainly track lexical cues.

title: Corrupting Ties: Investigating Robustness to Bias Injection Across Multi-Agent Network Topologies
summary: AI systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes decision-making contexts, where interactions among components can introduce fairness risks that remain undetected when auditing components or collective outcomes in isolation. As LLM-based multi-agent systems become more prevalent, understanding how biased information propagates through agent interactions is essential for assessing their fairness. We introduce a controlled bias injection framework that replaces selected agent responses with predefined biased ones, enabling an intervention-based analysis of how network topology and injection configurations shape system behavior. We propose decision divergence metrics that quantify the effects of these interventions at the agent, network, and system levels, and evaluate five topologies on three binary classification tasks using LLMs from the Qwen and Gemma families. Sequential networks show the greatest divergence, whereas fully connected and mesh networks show less. Injection position also matters: in star networks, injecting the central agent has larger effects than injecting peripheral agents. Models further differ in whether divergence follows the injected bias. These findings highlight the role of network structure in the propagation of biased information and motivate topology-aware auditing of fairness risks in multi-agent systems.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce a controlled bias injection framework for LLM-based multi-agent systems and find that sequential network topologies exhibit the greatest decision divergence while fully connected and mesh topologies are more robust.
AI.motivation: Interactions among components in LLM-based multi-agent systems can introduce fairness risks that remain hidden when auditing individual components or collective outcomes in isolation.
AI.method: The framework replaces selected agent responses with predefined biased ones and measures decision divergence at agent, network, and system levels across five topologies and three binary classification tasks using Qwen and Gemma models.
AI.result: Sequential networks show the greatest divergence, fully connected and mesh networks show less, and in star networks, injecting the central agent causes larger effects than injecting peripheral agents; models also differ in whether divergence follows the injected bias.
AI.conclusion: Network structure strongly governs how biased information propagates in multi-agent systems, motivating topology-aware fairness auditing.

title: SimAI: Mechanistic User Simulation through Psychological Network Models
summary: Realistic user simulation enables the study of human interactions when direct experimentation is costly or potentially harmful. However, existing simulators largely overlook the psychological mechanisms that drive user behavior. We introduce SimAI, a framework for mechanistic user simulation that models how psychological factors interact to shape user responses. To overcome the challenge of supervising open-ended behavior, we propose a graph reconstruction objective that provides graph-level rewards based on how well simulated conversations reflect the underlying psychological relationships. To support this approach, we construct PSYCHE, a dataset of 18,576 profile-network pairs derived from 516 psychotherapy cases. Automatic evaluations show that SimAI achieves greater simulation and behavioral diversity than existing patient simulators while maintaining strong profile alignment. In an interactive study with 30 mental-health professionals and trainees, SimAI receives the highest average ratings for conversational authenticity, realistic help-seeking behavior, and clinical training utility. Beyond simulation quality, SimAI enables realistic clinical training and uncovers safety failures in prolonged AI interactions with vulnerable users. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce SimAI, a mechanistic user simulation framework trained with a psychological graph reconstruction objective on the new PSYCHE dataset (18,576 profile-network pairs), achieving higher authenticity and behavioral diversity than existing patient simulators.
AI.motivation: Existing user simulators largely overlook the underlying psychological mechanisms that drive human behavior, limiting their realism for studying interactions and clinical training.
AI.method: SimAI models interactions among psychological factors and uses a graph reconstruction objective to provide graph-level rewards based on how well simulated conversations reflect underlying psychological relationships, supported by PSYCHE (18,576 profile-network pairs from 516 psychotherapy cases).
AI.result: SimAI outperforms existing patient simulators in simulation and behavioral diversity while maintaining strong profile alignment, and received the highest average ratings for conversational authenticity, realistic help-seeking, and clinical training utility from 30 mental-health professionals and trainees.
AI.conclusion: Mechanistic psychological modeling enables realistic clinical training and helps uncover safety failures in prolonged AI interactions with vulnerable users.

title: TUSI: A Citation-Grounded Graph-Based Benchmark
summary: Evaluating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems in Persian law remains challenging because benchmarks lack realism, grounding, and coverage of legal reasoning. Existing resources are either synthetically generated from statutory texts, lacking natural information needs, or derived from informal legal question--answer sources without explicit linkage to authoritative legal documents, making them unsuitable for rigorous evaluation of grounded legal reasoning. To address this gap, we introduce TUSI-Bench, a structured Persian legal benchmark designed for the evaluation of RAG-based systems. TUSI-Bench is built upon a multi-layered legal knowledge framework containing 7,261 legal articles and integrating codified statutes, legal commentaries, doctrinal writings, and Supreme Court unification rulings. We also construct a legal knowledge graph linking articles and concepts for structure-aware retrieval. Based on this foundation, TUSI-Bench provides two complementary evaluation tasks: (i) TUSI-QA, an open-ended question answering benchmark containing 1,999 questions that requires grounded responses with explicit legal citations, and (ii) TUSI-Bar, a multiple-choice benchmark containing approximately 500 four-option questions derived from Iranian Bar examination questions. Furthermore, we propose a graph-based retrieval baseline that leverages relational structure within the legal knowledge graph. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating graph-based relations improves retrieval recall by up to 8 percentage points compared to standard baselines, highlighting the importance of structured legal representations for RAG systems. The proposed benchmark provides a standardized resource for evaluating grounded legal reasoning in Persian and enables future research on structured legal intelligence.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce TUSI-Bench, a citation-grounded Persian legal RAG benchmark with 7,261 legal articles, a legal knowledge graph, and two evaluation tasks (TUSI-QA and TUSI-Bar), showing that graph-based retrieval improves recall by up to 8 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Existing Persian legal RAG benchmarks lack realism, explicit linkage to authoritative legal documents, and coverage of legal reasoning.
AI.method: TUSI-Bench integrates 7,261 legal articles (statutes, commentaries, doctrinal writings, Supreme Court rulings) into a legal knowledge graph and provides TUSI-QA (1,999 open-ended citation-grounded questions) and TUSI-Bar (~500 four-option Iranian Bar exam questions), alongside a graph-based retrieval baseline.
AI.result: Incorporating graph-based relations improves retrieval recall by up to 8 percentage points compared to standard baselines.
AI.conclusion: TUSI-Bench provides a standardized resource for evaluating grounded legal reasoning in Persian and demonstrates the value of structured legal representations for RAG.

title: Knowing Which, Not How Much: Language Models Order Party Positions They Cannot Place
comment: Accepted at the 40th Pacific Asia Conference on Language, Information and Computation (PACLIC 40)
summary: Language models are increasingly asked where real actors stand: what a party's platform prioritises, what an institution has committed to. Such judgments are gradable, carrying both an order and a magnitude. Nearly every benchmark that tests them asks about one entity at a time, then reads that score as the model's knowledge of the domain. Order and magnitude, however, need not be acquired together. Text about social entities carries far more comparison than measurement, so a model may hold a dependable ordering with no anchored scale beneath it. We ask whether a model can place a documented social position on a scale or only order the actors it compares, and what that means for how such knowledge is measured. We test this on party positions in Japan and South Korea, where the Comparative Manifesto Project's coded data supplies a rare external answer key. Asked to order four parties, models beat the strongest fixed-answer baseline by more than a factor of two; asked to place one party on the same scale, they fall below it. The ordering survives inside those failed placements, and supplying the coded values lifts placement to near ceiling. Comparative and absolute questions about the same fact therefore measure different things here, and for party issue salience a benchmark built from one cannot speak for the other.

AI.tldr: Testing LLMs on Japanese and South Korean political party positions, the authors show that models can accurately order parties comparatively even when they fail to place individual parties on an absolute scale.
AI.motivation: Benchmarks typically ask LLMs to place one entity at a time on a scale, assuming that order and magnitude knowledge are acquired together.
AI.method: Using Comparative Manifesto Project coded data for Japan and South Korea as ground truth, the authors compare LLM performance on ordering four parties versus placing a single party on the same scale.
AI.result: When ordering four parties, models beat the strongest fixed-answer baseline by more than a factor of two, whereas when placing one party on the same scale, they fall below it; supplying coded anchor values lifts placement to near ceiling.
AI.conclusion: Comparative and absolute questions about the same social facts measure distinct capabilities, so benchmarks built from one cannot speak for the other.

title: Call-Efficient ICD-10 Code Prediction via Supervised Candidate Generation and Selective LLM Invocation
summary: Automatic assignment of ICD-10 codes from short clinical diagnosis text is a practical medical text classification and normalization task. The task is difficult because diagnosis phrases are short and noisy, the ICD-10 label space is hierarchical, and the class distribution is strongly imbalanced. This paper presents a call-efficient ICD-10 code prediction pipeline that combines transformer embeddings, tree-based supervised candidate generation, candidate-level reranking, and a gated LLM assistance. The evaluation uses a leakage-safe validation protocol: model and threshold selection are based on out-of-fold cross-validation predictions, while final reporting is performed on a locked test set with no shared source-file groups. The supervised conditional parent-code candidate generator reaches 74.32% Top-1 accuracy on the locked test set and 93.05% Top-10 candidate coverage. A direct zero-shot GPT-5.6-Sol baseline reaches 81.01% Top-1 accuracy, but requires an invocation of this large model for every diagnosis. The final deployable system, Pre-LLM fusion, reaches 81.24% OOF-CV accuracy and 83.19% locked-test accuracy while calling the LLM for only 31.97% of cases. This improves the locked-test error rate from 25.68% for the supervised parent-code baseline to 16.81%, corresponding to a 34.5% relative error reduction. The results show that the most effective role of the LLM is controlled reranking on uncertain examples rather than unrestricted coding or full-dataset invocation.

AI.tldr: The authors present a call-efficient ICD-10 code prediction pipeline combining supervised candidate generation, reranking, and selective LLM invocation, achieving 83.19% locked-test accuracy while calling the LLM on only 31.97% of cases.
AI.motivation: Automatic ICD-10 coding from short, noisy clinical diagnosis text is challenging due to hierarchical labels and class imbalance, while invoking large LLMs on every case is costly.
AI.method: The pipeline combines transformer embeddings, tree-based supervised conditional parent-code candidate generation, candidate-level reranking, and gated LLM assistance, evaluated with out-of-fold cross-validation and a leakage-safe locked test set.
AI.result: The supervised candidate generator reaches 74.32% Top-1 accuracy and 93.05% Top-10 coverage; the final Pre-LLM fusion system reaches 83.19% locked-test accuracy (vs. 81.01% for zero-shot GPT-5.6-Sol) while invoking the LLM for only 31.97% of cases, a 34.5% relative error reduction over the supervised baseline.
AI.conclusion: Controlled LLM reranking on uncertain examples outperforms unrestricted full-dataset LLM invocation in both accuracy and call efficiency.

title: Latent Fact Composition under Next-Token Training
summary: Controlled studies of latent two-hop reasoning train transformers to predict only the answer, whereas language models are trained to predict every token. We ask whether a model trained on every token learns to answer two-hop questions whose intermediate entity appears in no two-hop training example. We build a synthetic corpus with such questions. On this corpus every term of the loss can be computed exactly. A looped transformer, a standard transformer and DiscoLoop answer almost none of these questions. We therefore introduce the Baton family of looped transformers. They pass the intermediate entity to the second loop as a token embedding. When trained to predict only the answer, two of its three variants answer these questions almost perfectly. We then relate the success and failure of each model to three design conditions. Experiments that change one condition at a time agree with this hypothesis. When Baton is trained on every token, however, its accuracy on these questions rises and then declines. We further split the gradient of the next-token loss into three terms. Removing the two terms that depend on the particular training set raises the peak accuracy but does not remove the decline. The decline arises in the second hop while the model still recalls both facts.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce the Baton family of looped transformers to study latent two-hop fact composition under next-token training, finding that while answer-only training succeeds, next-token training causes accuracy to rise and then decline due to second-hop degradation.
AI.motivation: Controlled studies of latent two-hop reasoning train models to predict only the answer, whereas standard language models are trained on every token.
AI.method: The authors build a synthetic corpus where intermediate entities never appear in two-hop training examples, propose Baton looped transformers that pass the intermediate entity as a token embedding to the second loop, and decompose the next-token loss gradient into three terms.
AI.result: Standard, looped, and DiscoLoop transformers fail on these questions; two of three Baton variants answer almost perfectly under answer-only training, but under next-token training accuracy rises and then declines in the second hop even though the model still recalls both facts.
AI.conclusion: Next-token training induces a second-hop composition decline in latent two-hop reasoning that is not eliminated by removing dataset-specific gradient terms.

title: DiagTrace: An Interactive Benchmark for Clinical Decision Making
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on medical question answering and diagnostic reasoning benchmarks. However, existing evaluations typically provide all patient information upfront and assess only the final diagnosis or rationale. This setup ignores the need to acquire diagnostic evidence incrementally from incomplete information in real-world diagnosis. To bridge this gap, we introduce DiagTrace, a source-grounded benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can reconstruct the documented diagnostic trajectory through interactive information seeking. Each benchmark instance is built from a PubMed Central case report and includes an initial presentation, an event bank, a clinical course, and diagnostic references. DiagTrace contains 510 cases across eight specialties, with 225 used to evaluate four LLMs on clinical-course alignment, interaction quality, and efficiency. Results reveal trade-offs in coverage, source-consistent ordering, and turn use.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce DiagTrace, an interactive benchmark of 510 PubMed Central clinical cases across eight specialties, evaluating whether LLMs can incrementally acquire diagnostic evidence from incomplete information.
AI.motivation: Existing medical QA benchmarks provide all patient information upfront and assess only final diagnoses, ignoring the incremental information-seeking required in real-world clinical decision making.
AI.method: Built from PubMed Central case reports, each DiagTrace instance includes an initial presentation, an event bank, a clinical course, and diagnostic references; 225 cases are used to evaluate four LLMs on clinical-course alignment, interaction quality, and efficiency.
AI.result: Evaluations across four LLMs reveal trade-offs among evidence coverage, source-consistent ordering, and turn efficiency.
AI.conclusion: DiagTrace enables source-grounded evaluation of interactive diagnostic trajectories rather than static final-answer accuracy.

title: GauntletScore: Auditable Fact-Checking That Matches the Best Published Checkers on LLM-AggreFact
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure, 7 tables. Per-claim predictions and scoring script: this https URL
summary: Checking whether a generated sentence is supported by its source document is a standard safeguard for AI-written text, and the strongest published checkers are single models. We describe GauntletScore, an evidence engine whose few rules and thresholds were set on the benchmark's development split. It puts typed questions to independent readers from different providers and records each answer as a measurement in an evidence ledger. It combines the measurements with a fixed Bayesian rule that counts a contradiction only when two readers agree. On the full LLM-AggreFact test split (29,320 claims across 11 datasets), following the leaderboard's approach, GauntletScore achieves 79.51 balanced accuracy, above every average published on the leaderboard as of 15 November 2026. That places it level with the best of them, nimble-v4-max (79.45 from its published dataset scores; the engine's 95% interval, 78.47 to 80.53, contains it). On the same claims it beats two of its three readers used alone (Readers A and B) by 1.66 and 2.17 points (95% intervals 0.80 to 2.53 and 1.29 to 3.06). Without AggreFact-CNN, described below, the leads are 0.90 and 1.32 and both intervals stay above zero. The engine also records the evidence behind every verdict, which a single model does not. Its largest margin is on full-length news articles checked against multi-sentence summaries (AggreFact-CNN), a format that resembles much regulated writing. There it scores 76.45, the best on the leaderboard, against 70.1 for the next best and 63.9 to 67.8 for the six systems with the highest averages. The test split was run once, on an engine frozen before the first test claim, under a stopping plan committed in advance. We release per-claim predictions and the scoring script.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce GauntletScore, an auditable fact-checking engine that combines typed questions to independent readers using a fixed Bayesian rule, achieving 79.51 balanced accuracy on LLM-AggreFact and 76.45 on AggreFact-CNN.
AI.motivation: Checking whether generated sentences are supported by source documents is dominated by single-model checkers that lack auditable evidence trails.
AI.method: GauntletScore poses typed questions to independent readers from different providers, logs answers in an evidence ledger, and combines them with a fixed Bayesian rule (tuned on dev) that counts a contradiction only when two readers agree.
AI.result: On the full LLM-AggreFact test split (29,320 claims across 11 datasets), GauntletScore achieves 79.51 balanced accuracy (matching nimble-v4-max at 79.45), beats two of its three individual readers by 1.66 and 2.17 points, and sets a new best of 76.45 on AggreFact-CNN (vs. 70.1 next best).
AI.conclusion: An auditable multi-reader evidence engine can match or surpass the strongest single-model fact-checkers while recording the exact evidence behind every verdict.

title: RLDE: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Interpretable Iterative Document Editing
summary: Improving the quality, clarity, and flow of long documents remains a challenging problem in NLP, as human editing typically occurs through iterative refinement rather than a single-pass rewrite. Most existing automated systems act as black-box generators or rely on supervised learning, limiting interpretability and failing to capture the sequential nature of revisions. In this paper, we propose RLDE, an automated end-to-end metric-driven RL framework that formulates document revision as a reference-free MDP problem (unsupervised with respect to paired document-revision targets). Working with a limited action space (NOOP, INSERT, DELETE, REPLACE), RLDE leverages Pointer Networks for dynamic span selection at the token level and sends generative actions to the frozen BART-base model to obtain context-aware suggestions. PPO agents learn to optimize a multi-objective reward function based on readability, perplexity, and grammar metrics with the help of a novel SBERT-based Semantic Preservation Penalty constraint to avoid deletion degeneracy. Evaluations on the BEA-2019 dataset showed statistically significant results (p < 0.01) across all metrics, where Flesch Reading Ease increased from 49.8 to 59.4, perplexity decreased from 63.7 to 39.8, while preserving 93% of semantic information. When compared to Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompt-engineered models like GPT-4 and LLaMA-2, RLDE shows high performance at a very low computational inference cost. Moreover, the quality of edits generated by RLDE has been verified via human evaluations, scoring 4.9/5 for meaning preservation and 4.4/5 for edit quality.

AI.tldr: The authors propose RLDE, an unsupervised reinforcement learning framework using Pointer Networks and a frozen BART-base model for iterative document editing, outperforming CoT-prompted GPT-4 and LLaMA-2 at lower inference cost.
AI.motivation: Human document editing is iterative, whereas most automated systems rely on black-box single-pass rewriting or supervised paired data, limiting interpretability and sequential refinement.
AI.method: RLDE formulates document revision as a reference-free MDP with actions (NOOP, INSERT, DELETE, REPLACE), using Pointer Networks for span selection, a frozen BART-base model for suggestions, and PPO optimizing readability, perplexity, grammar, and an SBERT-based Semantic Preservation Penalty.
AI.result: On BEA-2019, RLDE significantly (p < 0.01) improved Flesch Reading Ease from 49.8 to 59.4 and reduced perplexity from 63.7 to 39.8 while preserving 93% semantic information, and scored 4.9/5 for meaning preservation and 4.4/5 for edit quality in human evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Reference-free RL over discrete edit actions enables interpretable, low-cost iterative document editing without paired revision data.

title: Beyond Acuity Accuracy: A Multidimensional Framework for Evaluating Patient-Facing Emergency Triage AI Tools
comment: 82 pages, including 34 pages of supplementary material. 5 figures (4 main figures and 1 supplementary figure)
summary: Patient-facing AI triage tools may support care-seeking and emergency department prioritization, but require evaluation beyond acuity accuracy alone. We developed SAFE-Triage, a framework integrating human review, automated metrics, LLM-as-judge evaluation, and simulation testing across clinical performance, patient interaction, and clinician-facing summary quality. We applied SAFE-Triage to 40 MIMIC-IV-derived emergency vignettes and a 10,030-case acuity analysis comparing prompted LLM triage (PLT) with rule-augmented prompted LLM triage (rPLT). PLT achieved higher emergency severity index (ESI) accuracy (57.5% vs 42.8%, $P < 0.001$), lower undertriage (13.1% vs 29.8%, $P < 0.001$), and higher clinician ratings across all domains. rPLT produced shorter and more stable outputs with higher automated readability scores. SAFE-Triage identified trade-offs between acuity accuracy, undertriage risk, communication quality, readability, and summary quality, supporting pre-deployment refinement and ongoing monitoring by showing where triage tools are efficient, need improvement, or need clinician oversight.

AI.tldr: The authors develop SAFE-Triage, a multidimensional evaluation framework for patient-facing emergency triage AI tools, and show that prompted LLM triage achieves higher acuity accuracy and lower undertriage than rule-augmented triage, while revealing key communication and readability trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Patient-facing AI triage tools require evaluation beyond acuity accuracy alone, encompassing clinical safety, patient interaction, and clinician summary quality.
AI.method: SAFE-Triage integrates human review, automated metrics, LLM-as-judge evaluation, and simulation testing, applied to 40 MIMIC-IV vignettes and a 10,030-case acuity analysis comparing prompted LLM triage (PLT) with rule-augmented PLT (rPLT).
AI.result: PLT achieved higher ESI accuracy (57.5% vs. 42.8%, P < 0.001), lower undertriage (13.1% vs. 29.8%, P < 0.001), and higher clinician ratings across all domains, whereas rPLT produced shorter, more stable outputs with higher automated readability scores.
AI.conclusion: SAFE-Triage exposes critical trade-offs between acuity accuracy, undertriage risk, and communication quality to guide pre-deployment refinement and clinician oversight.

title: What MoE Routing Controls: Causal Interventions on Expert Trajectories
summary: In mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models, a token is routed to a sequence of experts across layers. We investigate how forcing tokens onto chosen expert paths influences model behavior. We build a target path from the experts that a concept's or role's tokens most often use, and we add a fixed bias to each target expert's router logit during generation to steer the token toward this expert path. We study two kinds of targets. Format targets concern the form of the output, and concept targets concern its topic. In Qwen3-30B-A3B, we show that steering a format path changes the text the model writes. We also show that steering a concept path shifts the model's next-token probabilities toward the concept, even when the path is built in another language, yet this shift has little effect on the generated text. We investigate why formats reach the text but concepts do not by steering only part of the generation, and find evidence that a format, once started, reinforces itself. We show that the concepts religion and money steer most strongly, and that the effect is concentrated in the middle layers. We attempt to explain why the strength of the effect varies by concept through an analysis of embedding distinctiveness and word frequency.

AI.tldr: By adding fixed biases to MoE router logits during generation in Qwen3-30B-A3B, the authors show that steering format expert paths alters generated text, whereas steering concept paths shifts next-token probabilities without reliably changing output text.
AI.motivation: In mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models, tokens follow expert trajectories across layers, but how causally forcing tokens onto chosen expert paths affects generation is unclear.
AI.method: The authors construct target expert paths from experts frequently used by a concept or format, add a fixed bias to target router logits during generation in Qwen3-30B-A3B, and test partial-generation steering and embedding/frequency analyses.
AI.result: Steering format paths changes generated text and reinforces itself once started; steering concept paths shifts next-token probabilities toward the concept (even cross-lingually) with little effect on generated text, with effects concentrated in middle layers and strongest for religion and money.
AI.conclusion: MoE routing exerts self-reinforcing control over output format while concept-level routing shifts primarily affect intermediate token probabilities rather than surface generation.

title: From Imperfective Paradox to Moorean Absurdity: Single-Chain Reasoning Lock-In and Multi-Candidate Verbalization Across Aspectual and Pragmatic Ambiguity
comment: 21 pages, 4 figures, 25 tables (single-column arXiv preprint; includes 16,640 Qwen3-8B formal units across 4 preregistered experiments, 1,800 OpenAI format-ablation calls, and 4,240 P16.7 development-slice units across 5 external models)
summary: Natural language entailment and coherence judgments often depend on whether an event merely occurred, reached a telic culmination, satisfied a plan, or was evaluated under multiple pragmatic standards. We test observable consequences of the single-chain premature lock-in hypothesis across four preregistered, sealed formal experiments on Qwen3-8B-Q8_0 (16,640 formal units, temperature=0.0): 15 of 16 hypothesis slots retain confirmatory status (12 rejecting H0 under within-experiment Holm control at alpha_fam=0.05; E3_H3 demoted to descriptive status). In Experiment 1, Direct-CoT vs. MCU differs by 25.00 pp on telic high-confidence completion (Holm p=1.31239e-05), while NLI-CoT collapses by -91.25 pp on uninterrupted atelic items (Holm p=1.81805e-21). Multi-Candidate Verbalization (MCV) elicits K=5 weighted estimates in one call, separating the prompt from unweighted (MCU) and self-weighted (MCW) readouts. Mandarin (E2) and English (E3) expose an Interruption-Anchored Realis Paradox under NLI-CoT. In Experiment 4, MCU-CF raises perceived coherence on implicit Moorean sentences by 26.64 pp over Direct-CoT (Holm p=0.0006), alongside Direct-CF - Direct-CoT = 29.15 pp and MCU-CoT - Direct-CoT = 17.31 pp. A 1,800-call OpenAI ablation and a stage="dev" P16.7 cross-model extension (4,240 planned/collected units across five external models: 4,222 valid, 18 format-missing, 0 transport-missing; <2% missing per slice; OpenAI gpt-4o-mini at top_logprobs=20 achieves 1,000/1,000 valid units) show that discrete NLI-CoT and scalar Direct-CoT judgments dissociate across models. Confirmatory effects concern observable prompt-and-readout protocols; internal premature lock-in remains a hypothesis. All code, stimuli, preregistered analysis plans, and verification tools are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Across four preregistered experiments on Qwen3-8B-Q8_0 (16,640 units) and a cross-model extension, the authors test the single-chain premature lock-in hypothesis using Multi-Candidate Verbalization (MCV), showing large divergences between discrete NLI-CoT and scalar/multi-candidate readouts.
AI.motivation: Natural language entailment and coherence judgments under aspectual and pragmatic ambiguity may suffer from premature lock-in when models commit to a single chain of thought.
AI.method: The authors run four preregistered experiments on Qwen3-8B-Q8_0 comparing Direct-CoT, NLI-CoT, and Multi-Candidate Verbalization (MCV, eliciting K=5 weighted estimates in one call with unweighted MCU and self-weighted MCW readouts), plus a 1,800-call OpenAI ablation and a 4,240-unit cross-model extension.
AI.result: Fifteen of 16 hypothesis slots retain confirmatory status (12 rejecting H0 under Holm control); Direct-CoT vs. MCU differs by 25.00 pp on telic completion, NLI-CoT collapses by -91.25 pp on uninterrupted atelic items, and MCU-CF raises coherence on implicit Moorean sentences by 26.64 pp over Direct-CoT.
AI.conclusion: Observable prompt-and-readout protocols strongly dissociate discrete NLI-CoT from scalar and multi-candidate judgments across models, though internal premature lock-in remains a hypothesis.

title: RISA: Recoverable Sparse Attention for Block-Diffusion Language Models
summary: Block-wise diffusion language models (DLMs) refine multiple tokens in parallel, offering an alternative to token-by-token autoregressive decoding. Their long-context inference, however, remains bottlenecked by memory-bound attention: every denoising step repeatedly reads a growing historical key--value (KV) cache.
