AI.conclusion: Exploiting estimator scale invariance across data batches provides a simple, broadly applicable route to robustly valid confidence sets.

title: Centroid Spectral Coupling: Implicit Alignment and Representation Diversity in Self-Supervised Learning
summary: Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) aims to align augmented views while preserving representation diversity and preventing collapse. Existing non-contrastive methods often address these goals using multiple weighted loss terms. We introduce Centroid Spectral Coupling (CSC), a single-term SSL objective that implicitly couples view alignment, representation diversity, and collapse resistance. CSC constructs centroids from independently normalized augmented-view pairs and applies a ridge-based spectral objective to their uncentered second-moment matrix. Preserving centroid magnitudes encodes view agreement while encouraging balanced representation energy across spectral directions. We establish an exact decomposition into nonnegative alignment and spectral-imbalance components, characterize the geometry of global optima, and derive finite-loss guarantees for alignment and diversity. We also show that complete constant-output collapse is a strict saddle in normalized representation space. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Imagenette show that CSC achieves the highest linear Top-1 accuracy among the evaluated non-contrastive methods on all three benchmarks, and the highest kNN Top-1 accuracy on both CIFAR datasets. A ridge-parameter sensitivity study reveals an empirical alignment--diversity trade-off: increasing $\kappa$ strengthens view alignment but reduces representation effective rank. These results show that a unified spectral objective yields competitive visual representations without explicit contrastive negatives or separately weighted alignment and diversity penalties.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Centroid Spectral Coupling (CSC), a single-term non-contrastive SSL objective that achieves top linear and kNN accuracy on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Imagenette.
AI.motivation: Non-contrastive self-supervised learning methods typically require multiple separately weighted loss terms to balance view alignment, representation diversity, and collapse prevention.
AI.method: CSC forms centroids from independently normalized augmented-view pairs and applies a ridge-based spectral objective to their uncentered second-moment matrix, with an exact decomposition into alignment and spectral-imbalance terms.
AI.result: CSC achieves the highest linear Top-1 accuracy among evaluated non-contrastive methods on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Imagenette, and the highest kNN Top-1 accuracy on both CIFAR datasets, while constant collapse is shown to be a strict saddle.
AI.conclusion: A single spectral objective on normalized view centroids implicitly couples alignment and diversity without contrastive negatives or multi-term loss tuning.

title: Training Neural Networks to be Locally Adaptive
summary: Deep neural networks fitted by global empirical risk minimization commit to a single model for the entire covariate space. In a regression problem, if the regression function $f_0$ is inhomogeneous --- varying rapidly in one region, while being nearly flat in another --- no single model can be appropriate everywhere, and the fit degrades where the function varies most rapidly. Here we study an alternative in which, instead of fitting the network globally, we fit it locally. For each query point $x$, a \emph{local neural network} is trained on the $k$ nearest-neighbours of $x$ alone, making the training sample and the fitted function query-dependent. We analyze the performance of the resulting estimator through a localization approach, establishing that the pointwise risk of the estimator with an appropriate choice of $k$ attains the rate $n^{-2\alpha/(2\alpha+d^{*})}$, up to logarithmic factors, when $f_0$ is locally $\alpha$-Hölder with $\alpha\in(0,1]$ and the covariates are supported on a $d^{*}$-dimensional manifold embedded in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$. A matching Le Cam lower bound shows that this rate is pointwise minimax optimal. However, the local rate-optimality requires $k$ to be calibrated to the smoothness of $f_0$, which is unknown in practice. We therefore provide a locally adaptive choice of $k$ that makes the neural network adapt to the local Hölder exponent of $f_0$ and to the intrinsic dimension simultaneously, both of which are potentially varying over the covariate domain. An extensive simulation study demonstrates the dominance of the locally adaptive neural network over a globally trained network and several state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: This paper studies local neural networks trained on k-nearest neighbors of each query point with a locally adaptive k, achieving pointwise minimax-optimal rates on inhomogeneous functions over manifolds.
AI.motivation: Globally trained neural networks commit to one model across the covariate space, degrading in regions where an inhomogeneous regression function varies rapidly.
AI.method: For each query point x, a local neural network is trained solely on its k nearest neighbors, with a locally adaptive selection of k that adapts simultaneously to the local Holder exponent alpha and intrinsic manifold dimension d*.
AI.result: With calibrated k, pointwise risk attains the minimax-optimal rate n^{-2alpha/(2alpha+d*)} up to logarithmic factors (matched by a Le Cam lower bound), and extensive simulations show the adaptive local network outperforms global networks and state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: Query-dependent local training with adaptive neighborhood sizing allows neural networks to adapt to spatially varying smoothness and intrinsic dimension.

title: The Price of Hard Coverage Constraints in Online Conformal Prediction
summary: Conformal prediction provides distribution-free uncertainty quantification, but in sequential deployment, standard coverage guarantees can still allow substantial fluctuations in the number of miscoverages over time. We study an online setting in which prediction sets are produced one round at a time and the cumulative number of miscoverages must stay within a prescribed budget throughout this http URL a hard coverage guarantee can be enforced by enlarging prediction sets, but how much additional prediction-set size is fundamentally necessary remains unclear. We characterize this unavoidable efficiency cost over $T$ prediction rounds. Remarkably, the cost persists even with i.i.d.\ data, a known score distribution, and perfect knowledge of the population-optimal prediction set. Under suitable regularity conditions relating coverage and prediction-set size, we determine the minimum cumulative excess prediction-set size required by any online method satisfying the hard coverage constraint. This minimum cost is $\Theta(\log T)$ for expected cost at a fixed time known in advance, $\Theta(T^{1/3})$ for the largest expected cost over all fixed times up to $T$, and $\Theta(\sqrt{T})$ for the expected worst realized cost when the evaluation time is chosen in hindsight. We further show that these rates can be attained using past scores, without knowing the score distribution. Thus, even perfect statistical knowledge does not make sequential reliability free.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes the unavoidable excess prediction-set size required to satisfy hard cumulative miscoverage constraints in online conformal prediction, proving tight rates from Theta(log T) to Theta(sqrt(T)).
AI.motivation: Standard online conformal guarantees allow large fluctuations in miscoverage counts, and the fundamental efficiency cost of enforcing a hard cumulative miscoverage budget over T rounds was unknown.
AI.method: The authors analyze the minimum cumulative excess prediction-set size over T rounds under regularity conditions, even when data are i.i.d. and the score distribution and optimal set are known, and construct distribution-free algorithms using past scores.
AI.result: The minimum excess size is Theta(log T) at a fixed known time, Theta(T^{1/3}) for the worst expected cost over fixed times up to T, and Theta(sqrt(T)) for expected worst realized cost in hindsight, all achievable without knowing the score distribution.
AI.conclusion: Hard sequential coverage constraints impose an unavoidable statistical price even under perfect distributional knowledge, though past-score algorithms can match the optimal rates.

title: TRAIL-IRL: Crossed Reward-Temperature Mixtures for Unlabeled Trajectory Clustering
summary: Different paths need not imply different preferences, trajectories also differ in how randomly actions are chosen. Many multi-reward inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) methods assume common action randomness and can confound it with preference heterogeneity. We introduce TRAIL-IRL, which clusters unlabeled trajectories using rewards for preferences and temperatures for action randomness. Its crossed mixture pairs each reward with a shared set of temperature levels, allowing action regularity to vary within preference groups. With centered and normalized rewards in a known finite-state environment, we establish the identifiability conditions under which the distribution of sufficiently long trajectories determines rewards, temperatures, mixing weights, and class counts up to relabeling. Under the same conditions and reward constraints, common-temperature reward mixtures with the same component count cannot reproduce a crossed mixture with multiple temperatures. We develop a generalized expectation-maximization algorithm and select class counts using the Bayesian information criterion (BIC). Simulations show improved predictive fit, reward recovery, and trajectory classification over common-temperature mixtures with the same component count. For 140 bird-year trajectories from 79 white storks, BIC favors four reward classes and three temperature levels over common-temperature candidates. Younger birds have higher posterior membership probabilities for a southwestward migration class, whereas older birds have higher probabilities for a northern retention class. Within reward classes, higher temperatures are associated with more variable movement directions and positions farther ahead along the migration route, consistent with social information use and collective sensing.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces TRAIL-IRL, a crossed reward-temperature mixture model for clustering unlabeled trajectories that separates preference heterogeneity from action randomness.
AI.motivation: Multi-reward inverse reinforcement learning methods typically assume uniform action randomness, confounding differences in stochasticity with differences in underlying reward preferences.
AI.method: TRAIL-IRL pairs each reward class with a shared set of temperature levels in a crossed mixture, establishes identifiability conditions in known finite-state environments, and fits parameters via generalized EM with BIC model selection.
AI.result: Simulations show better predictive fit, reward recovery, and clustering than common-temperature mixtures; on 140 white stork trajectories, BIC selects four reward classes and three temperatures, revealing age-linked migration classes and social-information-consistent temperature patterns.
AI.conclusion: Modeling crossed reward and temperature mixtures prevents confounding action randomness with preferences in unlabeled trajectory clustering.

title: Fold Weighting for Cross-Validation Under Continuous Distributional Drift
summary: Cross-validation weights all folds equally, so under drift the oldest folds count as much as the newest. We model drift by a Hölder condition in total variation distance and give finite-sample bounds on the excess deployment risk of the configuration that sliding-window cross-validation selects. Each bound splits into drift, estimation, and validation-noise terms. With equal weights the drift terms saturate as the record grows. With fold weights fixed in advance, the drift terms become weighted averages, which shrink as weight moves toward deployment. The noise term grows as the weights concentrate and shrinks with the batch size. The drift terms are linear in the weights and the noise term is convex, so minimizing the bound over the weights is a convex problem. Applications to U.S. earnings and flight delays show both sides of this trade-off. Weight on recent folds pays off when a change in the best predictor persists and each period has many observations, and equal weights do best when changes are short-lived.

AI.tldr: This paper derives finite-sample risk bounds for weighted sliding-window cross-validation under continuous distributional drift and formulates optimal fold-weight selection as a convex program.
AI.motivation: Standard cross-validation weights all folds equally, giving stale past folds as much influence as recent ones when data distributions drift continuously.
AI.method: Modeling drift via a Holder condition in total variation distance, the authors bound excess deployment risk in terms of drift, estimation, and validation-noise terms, and minimize the convex bound over pre-specified fold weights.
AI.result: In U.S. earnings and flight-delay applications, weighting recent folds improves performance when predictor changes persist and batch sizes are large, whereas equal weights perform best when changes are short-lived.
AI.conclusion: Convex optimization of fold weights formalizes the bias-variance trade-off between recency and validation noise in cross-validation under drift.

title: DeltaHarness: Self-Evolving Harnesses for Resource-Adaptive Tool Execution
summary: Tool-using agents rely on execution harnesses to organize and schedule tool operations. The same task and resource description can conceal runtime conditions that reverse the latency ordering of valid execution plans. Resolving this uncertainty requires firsthand execution in the target setting. We introduce DeltaHarness, an execution-guided policy-search method that adapts agent harnesses from cold-start measurements. Its QHI loop uses the observed response to update runtime dispatch, revise physical plans, and select experiments for later proposals. An independent confirmation panel controls policy replacement. With fixed dispatch, a revised materialization policy reduces complete-delivery latency by 30.0% on one video-editing task across three fresh pairs. On held-out tasks, the evolved policies reduce latency by 8.2% relative to the best fixed plan in one seed and by 4.6% relative to the initial proposal in another.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces DeltaHarness, an execution-guided policy-search method that adapts tool-execution harnesses from cold-start runtime measurements, cutting task latency by up to 30.0%.
AI.motivation: Identical task and resource descriptions can hide runtime conditions that reverse the latency ordering of valid tool-execution plans, requiring firsthand execution to resolve.
AI.method: DeltaHarness runs a QHI loop that uses observed execution responses to update runtime dispatch, revise physical plans, and select experiments, governed by an independent confirmation panel for policy replacement.
AI.result: A revised materialization policy cuts complete-delivery latency by 30.0% on a video-editing task across three fresh pairs, and evolved policies reduce held-out task latency by 8.2% over the best fixed plan in one seed and 4.6% over the initial proposal in another.
AI.conclusion: Closed-loop execution-guided harness adaptation enables tool-using agents to discover lower-latency execution plans under real runtime conditions.

title: AdaFlowLite: Scalable and Non-blocking Inference on Asynchronous Mobile Data
summary: The rise of mobile devices equipped with numerous sensors, such as LiDAR and cameras, has driven the adoption of multi-modal deep intelligence for distributed sensing tasks, such as smart cabins and driving assistance. However, the arrival time of mobile sensory data vary due to modality size and network dynamics, which can lead to delays (if waiting for slow data) or accuracy decline (if inference proceeds without waiting). Moreover, the diversity and dynamic nature of mobile systems exacerbate this challenge. In response, we present a shift to \textit{opportunistic} inference for asynchronous distributed multi-modal data, enabling inference as soon as partial data arrives. While existing methods focus on optimizing modality consistency and complementarity, known as modal affinity, they lack a \textit{computational} approach to control this affinity in open-world mobile environments. % \sysname pioneers the formulation of structured cross-modality affinity in mobile contexts using a hierarchical analysis-based normalized matrix. This approach accommodates the diversity and dynamics of modalities, generalizing across different types and numbers of inputs. Employing an multi-modal lightweight Swin Transformer (MMLST), \sysname facilitates real-time and flexible data imputation, adapting to various modalities and downstream tasks without retraining. Experiments show that \sysname significantly reduces inference latency by up to 80.4\% and enhances accuracy by up to 62.1\%, while achieving nearly a 50\% reduction in energy consumption, outperforming status quo approaches. Also, this method can enhance LLM performance to preprocess asynchronous data.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an opportunistic non-blocking inference framework for asynchronous mobile multi-modal data using a normalized cross-modality affinity matrix and a lightweight Swin Transformer.
AI.motivation: Varying arrival times across mobile sensors force existing systems to either incur high latency waiting for slow modalities or lose accuracy by proceeding without them.
AI.method: The framework formulates structured cross-modality affinity via a hierarchical analysis-based normalized matrix and uses a multi-modal lightweight Swin Transformer (MMLST) for real-time data imputation across varying modalities without retraining.
AI.result: Experiments show up to 80.4% lower inference latency, up to 62.1% higher accuracy, and nearly 50% lower energy consumption compared to status quo approaches, while also enhancing LLM preprocessing of asynchronous data.
AI.conclusion: Opportunistic inference with structured cross-modality affinity and lightweight imputation enables fast, accurate, and energy-efficient mobile multi-modal intelligence under asynchronous sensor arrivals.
